content.p: For five weeks in the spring of 1986, a couple living in an ordinary house in Willagee, a southern suburb of Perth, abducted women and girls, held them at home and killed four of them. David Birnie and Catherine Birnie were both given life sentences. The case is often called the Moorhouse murders, after their address at 3 Moorhouse Street.

It came to an end because a 17-year-old, Kate Moir, escaped from the house on 10 November 1986 and was, at first, not believed by most of the police who heard her. David Birnie died in prison in 2005. Catherine Birnie has been in prison ever since, and the question of whether she should ever be released has kept the case in Western Australian politics for years.

The West Australian reported that Catherine Harrison met David Birnie when both were 12 and that they were sweethearts by 16, against her parents' wishes. Their early relationship was marked by repeated trouble with the law. She later married Donald McLaughlin and had seven children, then left him and the family weeks after the birth of her seventh child to live with David. They never married, but she took his surname. The Sydney Morning Herald put the move at 1985 and said she left six children.

The same newspaper wrote that for about a year the couple rehearsed fantasies of rape and murder before acting on them. Author Ruth Wykes, quoted by The Line Up, said "There was nothing random about what they did." The couple had planned to bury victims in a national park, the site reported, and had a code phrase to signal that Catherine approved of a woman as a target.
Sources disagree on some dates and details. The sequence below follows a PerthNow timeline, with differences noted.

Mary Neilson. Neilson, a 22-year-old psychology student at the University of Western Australia, wanted cheaper tyres for her car. David worked at a spare-parts business and invited her to the house. PerthNow dates this to 11 October; The Line Up and The West Australian say 6 October. She was held and raped, driven to Gleneagles forest and killed, and buried in a shallow grave. According to The Line Up, her car was then left near police headquarters.

Susannah Candy. Candy was a Hollywood Senior High School student abducted while hitchhiking on Stirling Highway at Claremont, about two weeks later. PerthNow gives her age as 15 and the date as 23 October; The West Australian calls her 16. She was taken to the house and forced to write letters to her family saying she was well, a tactic the Birnies repeated with later victims, according to The Line Up. The West Australian reported that David urged Catherine to prove her devotion by killing the girl, and that Catherine later recounted that she had done it to see "how strong I was within my inner self". She was buried near Neilson.

Noelene Patterson. Patterson, 31, was a bar manager at Nedlands Golf Club. Her car ran out of petrol on Canning Highway on 1 November, according to PerthNow, and the Birnies picked her up. The West Australian said she was kept for three days and that a jealous Catherine told David to kill her or she would do it herself. David drugged and strangled her. She was buried at Gleneagles.

Denise Brown. Brown, 21, was waiting for a bus on Stirling Highway on 5 November. PerthNow and The West Australian agree that she was held at Moorhouse Street and taken to a pine plantation the next day, naming it respectively as Gnangara and Wanneroo. They believed they had killed her and began to bury her, but she sat up in the grave, and David struck her with an axe. She died there.

Kate Moir was 17. According to Mamamia, she accepted a lift home on 9 November after a night out; PerthNow says she was picked up on Stirling Highway at Nedlands after an evening in Claremont. Moir was held at knifepoint, taken to Moorhouse Street and raped by David while Catherine watched and took notes, WAtoday reported on the basis of the Channel Seven programme Murder Uncovered.

Moir later said she understood within about two hours that her chances were slim: "You know you're gonna die but you don't acknowledge that to yourself, you just live it." She was forced to phone her mother. Knowing her mother would find it strange, she said she had been drinking and was staying at a friend's, hoping that she would grow suspicious, The West Australian wrote. She was offered pills to help her sleep, hid them under her tongue and then under the mattress, and slept with her foot handcuffed to David's.

The next morning David went to work. Catherine went to the door, and Moir broke a window lock and climbed out. WAtoday said Catherine had been distracted by a knock; The West Australian said she had gone to the door for a drug deal. Moir ran to neighbours' doors, was attacked by a dog, and found a man at a shop. By her account, she told him, "If a woman comes here and says I've had a fight with her and I'm her daughter, don't believe her."

At Palmyra Police Station, Moir's account was met with scepticism. Constable Laura Hancock, 22, had never taken a statement before, and was the only woman on duty. She told Murder Uncovered that she had been told it was a "bizarre story" and was instructed to "stitch her up" for a false report. Hancock said she was convinced by the detail: Rocky was in the video recorder, a Dire Straits tape was in the stereo, and Moir had drawn pictures and hidden them in the house to show she had been there. The Birnies had used false names, but Moir had seen a medicine bottle bearing the name David Birnie, PerthNow reported. Hancock said she left the room several times to press her superiors. PerthNow reported that major crime detectives took over only when Moir mentioned the name David Birnie, who by then had a long criminal record.

Police searched the house the following day. PerthNow reported that Catherine had burned evidence in the fireplace on David's instruction after Moir's escape, but that officers found chains and handcuffs in the main bedroom and the hidden sleeping pills, as Moir had described. In separate interviews David said he had picked up a hitchhiker and that sex had been consensual, and Catherine said she had never met the girl. Detective Vince Katich then bluffed David that police should get shovels and dig up the graves. David gave way and said there were four. Both Birnies led police to the graves of Neilson, Candy, Patterson and Brown, PerthNow reported.

The Line Up reported that David confessed to the four murders and pleaded guilty, and that Catherine was found guilty. Sources describe the penalties differently. David received life imprisonment under strict security. Catherine's sentence is reported as four life terms by The Line Up and The West Australian, and as life with a 20-year minimum by PerthNow. Her minimum expired in 2007.

The lead detective, Paul Ferguson, later said of Catherine Birnie that she had never given the victims "one ounce of consideration", and described the couple as "the most evil people I've ever, ever come across."

David Birnie was held in a protection division at Casuarina Prison. A former guard, Adrian Commons, told PerthNow that he was a "model prisoner" who raised an injured pigeon and fed a feral cat. WAtoday reported that the couple exchanged more than 2,600 letters but were allowed no other contact.

On 7 October 2005 he was found hanging in his cell at about 4:30 a.m. A coronial inquest in December 2007 heard that he had planned the method for some time. A police officer told the inquiry there was no evidence of foul play or of a failure of duty of care. It also heard that he had lost his computer after pornographic images were found on it, that he was implicated in the sexual assault of another prisoner and that his antidepressant dose had been cut off three days earlier because paperwork had not arrived. The newspaper gave his age as 54 in 2007 and as 55 on the day of death in 2005. Catherine was not allowed to attend his funeral.

Catherine Birnie's case came before the Prisoners Review Board every three years. In 2007 an assessment found a low risk of reoffending, but Attorney-General Jim McGinty said she should never be freed, because of the extreme nature of the crimes. In March 2010 his successor, Christian Porter, kept her in prison and did not put her on parole or in a re-socialisation program. In 2013 Michael Mischin accepted a board recommendation to keep her inside for another three years, and in March 2016 he did so again, citing the board's recommendation in her fourth review since her minimum term ended.

Public argument split. Perth lawyer Tom Percy QC called her a "church mouse" working in the prison library and said keeping her locked up was "pure revenge", according to PerthNow. Her youngest son Peter, who was six when she left, told Channel Seven he did not want her freed and that he had cut contact. Yahoo News reported that she had starred in a prison production of the musical Nunsense.

Moir campaigned in 2016 to end automatic three-yearly parole reviews. X-Press Magazine reported her claim of more than 13,000 petition signatures in five weeks. In October 2018 Attorney-General John Quigley introduced a bill to let the Attorney-General order parole consideration suspended for up to six years, extendable by six more. He said it would spare victims' families the trauma of repeated hearings. The Canberra Times reported that a Murdoch University law professor, Guy Hall, saw "an element of grandstanding" in it. SBS said Birnie, then 66, was due for review in 2019. The sources opened here do not say what happened to that bill or to later reviews.

The Guardian wrote that the case had become an "archetypal" Australian horror, and that the 2016 film Hounds of Love drew comparisons with it, though its director said he had drawn on nine killer couples. Moir said she felt "taken advantage of" and wanted the Birnies "forgotten". The West Australian noted in 2022 that the Moorhouse Street house still stands.
